summary: This experimental RFC extends OLSRv2, a routing protocol for wireless mesh networks, so one network can maintain several separate routing topologies at once. It stays interoperable with OLSRv2 routers that do not support the extension. It also updates RFC 7188 and RFC 7631 by changing their TLV registries and descriptions.

eli5.summary: Imagine one town with separate road maps for cars, bikes and buses. This lets wireless routers keep several maps at once, while old routers that only know one map still work fine.

subtitle: How OLSRv2 wireless mesh routers can keep one routing table per link metric while staying compatible with plain OLSRv2.

tldr.problem: OLSRv2 uses a single link metric type for all routes, but some mobile ad hoc networks would benefit from routing different traffic using different metrics.
tldr.mechanism: Each router picks a set of link metric types per interface, advertises them in a new MPR_TYPES TLV, and maintains separate metrics, MPR choices and a separate Routing Set for each type.
tldr.outcome: It is an Experimental extension that works alongside OLSRv2 routers without it, published to gather operational experience before any move to the Standards Track.

facts.label: New message TLV
facts.value: MPR_TYPES (Type Extension 1 of the MPR_WILLING type)

today: RFC 7722 is an Experimental RFC. It updates RFC 7188 and RFC 7631, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes it. The text says it is published to gather experience, with a possible later proposal for the Standards Track.

sections.title: Introduction and Motivation
sections.content:
The Optimized Link State Routing Protocol version 2 (OLSRv2, RFC 7181) is a proactive link state routing protocol for Mobile Ad Hoc Networks (MANETs). It can use link metrics to choose routes other than minimum-hop routes, but it uses a single link metric type for all routes.

This extension, called MT-OLSRv2, lets a router maintain multiple Routing Sets, one for each link metric type it supports, while keeping maximal interoperability with OLSRv2 routers that do not implement it. The RFC notes that multi-topology routing is a natural extension to link state protocols such as OSPF, but for OLSRv2 it does not yet have extensive operational or experimental experience.

The document is published to collect that experience, and it asks for reports on mixed networks, dynamic topologies, realistic deployments, which metric types were useful, and resource requirements. The intent is to propose the extension for the Standards Track once enough evidence exists.
sections.eli5: Normally every router in the network draws just one kind of map. This RFC lets routers draw several maps, such as the fastest road or the safest road, and asks people to try it and report back.

sections.title: Where It Applies
sections.content:
MT-OLSRv2 applies to any MANET where OLSRv2 applies, but in which several topologies are kept, each tied to a different link metric type. The network layer is assumed, but left outside the scope, to choose which topology each packet uses, for example by Differentiated Services Code Point (RFC 2474).

That choice MUST be consistent: every router that receives a packet must pick the same link metric type, so each packet follows a single topology and cannot loop. Meanings of link metric types are up to the MANET operator. They could stand for packets of different types, different stream rates, or different trust requirements.
sections.eli5: Every router has to agree which map a particular package should follow. If they disagree, the package could go in circles.

sections.title: How Multiple Topologies Work
sections.content:
The single router parameter LINK_METRIC_TYPE is replaced by an interface array IFACE_METRIC_TYPES and a router array ROUTER_METRIC_TYPES, the union of all interface arrays. Neither may contain repeats. If the deployment might include non-MT-OLSRv2 routers, LINK_METRIC_TYPE MUST be the first element of both. The willingness parameter WILL_ROUTING becomes an array with one value per metric type.

In the information bases, many single values (metrics, willingness, MPR status, hop counts) become maps from metric type to value. A separate Routing Set is kept for every type in ROUTER_METRIC_TYPES, calculated as in RFC 7181 using the value for that type. Entries whose metric is UNKNOWN_METRIC are ignored.

Routing MPRs (multipoint relays) are calculated for each metric type, ignoring links that do not support it. Flooding MPR decisions are left to each router, but MUST still reach the same symmetric 2-hop neighbors as a router without MT-OLSRv2 would.
sections.eli5: Each router keeps a list of the kinds of maps it knows, and a separate notebook of notes for each kind. Entries it knows nothing about are simply skipped.

sections.title: TLVs, HELLO and TC Messages
sections.content:
A new MPR_TYPES message TLV (the same type as MPR_WILLING with Type Extension 1) carries one octet per supported metric type. A message MUST NOT contain more than one. If non-MT-OLSRv2 routers may be present, the first octet MUST be LINK_METRIC_TYPE, and it may be omitted when that would be the only type. HELLO messages list the types on the sending interface, and TC messages list the router's types.

The MPR_WILLING value is extended with additional 4-bit willingness sub-fields, in the same order as MPR_TYPES. The LINK_METRIC TLV is unchanged but its Type Extension range is extended to 0-7. The MPR TLV value becomes a variable-length bitfield with one flooding bit and one routing bit per metric type, and the GATEWAY TLV may carry one hop count octet per type. In both, the first octet stays compatible with plain OLSRv2.

On receipt, if non-MT-OLSRv2 routers might exist and the first reported metric type is not LINK_METRIC_TYPE, the HELLO or TC message MUST be silently discarded. Shorter MPR_WILLING values are read as WILL_NEVER, so older routers never act as routing MPR for unknown metrics.
sections.eli5: Each message now says which kinds of maps the sender knows, in a fixed order. The first one is always the kind old routers understand, so they can still read the beginning.

sections.title: Management Considerations
sections.content:
A network using MT-OLSRv2 usually needs more management than plain OLSRv2. Operators must decide which link metric, and so which Routing Set, applies to each received packet, and all routers MUST decide the same way for the same packet. One suggested approach is to map each DSCP to a single metric. They must also choose which metrics each interface supports, and keep the network sufficiently connected. A poor collective choice can make the MANET anywhere from inefficient to nonfunctional.

If non-MT-OLSRv2 routers exist, the network is connected to the maximum extent using LINK_METRIC_TYPE, but that only delivers packets using that metric. Such routers SHOULD only send packets that use that topology. A packet routed on a topology a router is not part of will not loop. It is either dropped or routed onward by an MT-OLSRv2 router.
sections.eli5: Someone has to decide which map each kind of package uses, and make sure enough routers know each map. Otherwise some packages may get stuck.

sections.title: IANA and Security
sections.content:
IANA actions change the Message TLV Type 7 extensions by adding MPR_TYPES as Type Extension 1 and updating the MPR_WILLING description. They also change the MPR TLV bit descriptions and the GATEWAY TLV description, and allocate Type Extensions 0-7 of the LINK_METRIC TLV as assigned by administrative action, with 8-223 left to Expert Review. This is why the RFC updates RFC 7188 and RFC 7631.

On security, the mechanisms and requirements of RFC 7181 apply directly. The extension adds no new vulnerabilities, because each link metric type is used independently and could have been the only type used by an RFC 7181 implementation. Information of an unsupported type is ignored by all routers.
sections.eli5: The registry of reserved labels gets a few new entries. Safety rules stay the same as before, because each map is used on its own.
